title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Furniture restoration
audience: Any home-service operator, including solo operators, starting or growing a business.
learningOutcomes: Write an offer with a clear promised outcome, time frame and conditions
Identify the friction and risk the customer carries and reduce them
Price the offer on value and cost, not only time

instruction.heading: A bad offer versus a good offer
instruction.body: "I will restore your dining chairs" is a service. "I will inspect the set, give you one fixed price for the agreed repairs and finish within the agreed days, and redo any finish that fails the agreed sheet at no charge" is an offer. The customer buys a restored piece they can use, and the certainty that the price will not change without their agreement.

instruction.heading: The five parts of an offer
instruction.body: Set a clear outcome, such as a repaired and refinished set of chairs with a named finish; a time frame, such as the days the pieces are in the workshop; the work the customer must do, such as choosing the finish and approving the inspection quote; the certainty you give, such as an inspection report with photos; and the risk you carry. Put the scope and exclusions in writing, because a written quote can become binding once it is accepted (business.gov.au, 1 August 2025).

instruction.heading: Inspect first, then give a fixed price
instruction.body: Furniture prices depend on size and damage, so the offer should separate the inspection from the restoration. The Airtasker guide says furniture restoration prices usually depend on the size and damage of the piece (Airtasker, last updated 17 April 2025). The research found no sourced inspection fee, so set your own fee, state it before the visit, and credit it against the job if that is your policy. Once the inspection is done, put one fixed price in writing for the agreed scope. Any damage found later is priced as a change, with the customer's agreement first.

instruction.heading: Stepped options for the same piece
instruction.body: A stepped structure lets the customer choose the level of work. A repair and clean may be the first step, and a full strip and refinish the next, with each higher level adding something the customer can see, such as new hardware or a hand-finished top. Stepped packages are one way to lay out an offer (Jobber Academy, updated 8 October 2024). Show the steps as separate lines, each with its scope, so the customer can compare them.

instruction.heading: Guarantees and claims
instruction.body: The Australian Consumer Law consumer guarantees apply to services. They require due care and skill, delivery within a reasonable time where none is agreed, and fitness for any stated purpose, and a business cannot remove them by contract or notice (ACCC, last modified 17 July 2026). A finish warranty that you add is an extra promise on top of those guarantees (business.gov.au, 27 May 2025). Do not promise that a piece will last a set number of years or will never mark, because the research found no verified product or finish warranty rule for furniture.

instruction.heading: Price the offer as one total
instruction.body: Show one total for each piece, and one total for the job, and say whether GST is included. The ACCC's price display guidance (2 October 2026) says the total must include unavoidable fees. Pickup and delivery that are unavoidable for the job belong in that total, or on a separate line that is clearly shown.

procedure: Write the restored outcome for each piece in one sentence a customer would repeat.
Set a time frame for each piece that you have checked against your own completed jobs, and record how often you meet it.
Inspect the piece and record its size, damage and finish in writing before any price is given.
Add one certainty element, such as an inspection report with photos and a signed scope sheet.
Decide the guarantee and the finish warranty, and check that you can afford each one.
Price each piece from the inspection, then check the rate against cost and time.

workedExamples.situation: A family brings in a dining table and four chairs. The Airtasker guide lists a dining table at $500 to $1,100 and a dining chair at $50 to $100, and it says prices usually depend on size and damage. The unit is not stated, but the table reads as a per-item price.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the offer present the set, and what happens before a fixed price is given?
workedExamples.reasoning: The offer shows each item on its own line, after an inspection. The table and the four chairs are inspected, and each is given its own fixed price for the agreed scope. The sourced ranges can help the family see the spread: the table at $500 to $1,100 and four chairs at $200 to $400 together. That combined $700 to $1,500 is an arithmetic sum of two item ranges, not a sourced job price. The range is wide because damage drives price, so the inspection is what moves each item into a band.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: during stripping of a chair, the owner finds a cracked joint that was not visible at inspection.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the owner do before continuing?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner stops and tells the client what has been found, with photos. The repair is priced as a change to the agreed scope, and the client agrees in writing before the work continues. The offer's exclusions already say that hidden damage found after inspection is priced as a change. The owner does not carry on and absorb the cost unless that is a stated policy.

equipmentAndPpe: Inspection sheet with size, damage, finish and photos
Scope sheet listing each piece, its repairs and its finish
Written warranty template, kept separate from the consumer guarantees
Safety data sheet for every stripper and finish used (see the safety section)

commonErrors.error: Giving a fixed price before inspecting the piece.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect first, record the findings with photos, and then give one fixed price for the agreed scope.

commonErrors.error: Treating a per-item range as a per-hour rate, or the reverse. Gap: the Airtasker unit is not stated.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the unit beside every rate, and confirm it before the quote is sent.

commonErrors.error: Promising a finish that will never mark, or a life of years.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the finish on the scope sheet in terms you can demonstrate, and state any warranty as an extra promise in writing.

commonErrors.error: Absorbing hidden damage without telling the client.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the finding, and price the change for the client's agreement before continuing.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Consumer guarantees for services apply under the Australian Consumer Law, and a business cannot exclude them by contract (ACCC, 17 July 2026). Business guidance only: this lesson does not grant any licence or authority.

NSW only: NSW LeadSmart (modified 20 July 2026) says lead paint was used in most homes built in Australia before 1970, and that furniture may carry it. It recommends a professional trained in lead paint work for stripping, and says wet sanding and wet scraping are the safest methods. Open-flame torches should not be used. Check the lead rules that apply in your state before quoting any stripping job on old painted furniture.
Show one total price for each piece and the job, including unavoidable fees, as the ACCC price display guidance requires (2 October 2026).

qualityStandard: Offer and pricing decisions are written down and checked against cost and time.
documentationEvidence: Written offer or plan, evidence collected, and the decision made.
summary: A furniture offer inspects first, then gives one fixed price for the agreed scope.
Prices depend on size and damage, so the inspection is part of the offer, not an extra.
Gap: the Airtasker unit is not stated, and no inspection fee, trade body or dealer or auction referral channel is verified.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which part of a furniture restoration offer does the customer buy?
options: A restored piece, with an inspected fixed price and certainty

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a furniture offer separate the inspection from the restoration?
options: Because damage found on inspection changes the scope and the price
Because customers never ask for a quote
Because the ACCC forbids any quote for furniture
Because inspection replaces the written scope

knowledgeChecks.question: Old painted furniture may contain lead. What does the NSW guidance recommend for stripping?
options: Wet methods and a professional trained in lead paint work
An open-flame torch, to speed up the stripping
Dry sanding in a closed room
No precautions, if the paint looks sound
